name: Lip scrub exfoliation

lead: A lip scrub rubs flaking skin off the lips so they look smoother and take balm or lipstick more evenly. The smoothing is visible right away.

Sugar or salt grains physically remove surface skin cells, which is a form of mechanical exfoliation. No studies of lip scrubs specifically were found. Dermatologists quoted on Wikipedia say exfoliation is not medically necessary because skin sheds on its own, and that lip licking and weather are common causes of chapping.

paras: People rub the scrub gently over the lips, rinse or wipe it off, and follow with balm or petroleum jelly. It is commonly done before applying lip color, and some do it once or twice a week.
Dermatologists quoted on Wikipedia say over-exfoliating can weaken the skin barrier and cause redness and sensitivity. Rough scrubbing on already cracked lips can cause irritation.

chain: Smoother lips that hold color better
angle.text: Users rub on sugar or salt scrubs to clear flaking skin so lips look smoother and take balm or color more evenly. The smoothing is visible right away. No studies test lip scrubs specifically.

lead: A lip scrub is an abrasive product, commonly sugar- or salt-based, used to rub flaking skin off the lips. People use it to get smoother, softer-looking lips so that lip balm, lipstick or gloss goes on evenly, and to remove visible flakes that can make the lips look dry or uneven.[1][2]

It is a form of mechanical exfoliation, in which abrasives such as sugar or salt crystals, cloths or brushes physically remove surface skin cells; the alternative is chemical exfoliation with acids or enzymes.[1] Lip skin is thin, with only about three to five cell layers compared with up to 16 in facial skin, and has no hair and no sweat glands, which is why lips dry out and chap more easily than other skin.[3]

Dermatologists quoted on Wikipedia say manual or chemical exfoliation is not medically necessary because skin sheds dead cells on its own, and that overdoing it can weaken the skin barrier and cause sensitivity and redness.[1] Wikipedia's article on cheilitis lists lip licking and weather as common causes of chapped lips and describes barrier lubricants such as lip balm or petroleum jelly as the usual treatment.[4][2]
infobox: About 3 to 5 cell layers; no hair or sweat glands[3]

paras: Mechanical exfoliation uses abrasives such as microfiber cloths, scrubs, crushed shells, sugar or salt crystals, pumice, sponges, loofahs and brushes. Chemical exfoliation uses alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic and lactic acid, beta hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid, or enzymes to loosen dead cells.[1] Lip scrubs belong to the mechanical group, and some products pair the abrasive with oils or butters.

Home-made versions are usually sugar or salt mixed with an oil or honey-type base, while commercial products add flavours and butters. Lip skin is thin [3], and lip care routines commonly follow exfoliation with a balm [2].

Lips lack sweat glands and the oil layer that normally keeps skin smooth, so they dry and chap quickly.[3] Wikipedia's lip balm article lists cold, dry or windy weather, lip licking and mouth breathing as causes of chapping, and says balms form an occlusive layer that seals in moisture.[2] Common balm bases include beeswax, candelilla and carnauba wax, lanolin and petrolatum.[2]

Wikipedia's cheilitis article describes chapped lips as the most common type of lip inflammation, usually on the lower lip, with cracking, peeling and fissures; contributing factors include cold dry weather, sun and lip licking, and saliva's digestive enzymes and evaporation can dry the lips further. Barrier products such as lip balm or petroleum jelly usually help [4]. A rarer condition, exfoliative cheilitis, shows continuous shedding of thick scales on the red border of the lips; its cause is unknown but it has been linked to stress, thyroid dysfunction and repetitive lip licking or picking, and it is managed by moisturising and topical corticosteroids [4].

Lip balm is older than lip scrubs. Wikipedia reports that Egyptians made lip care from beeswax, olive oil and animal fat around 40 BC, that physician Charles Browne Fleet invented the modern lip balm and named it ChapStick in the 1880s, and that Carmex appeared in Milwaukee in 1937 [2]. Bonne Bell launched the first flavoured lip balm under the Lip Smackers name in 1973, Burt's Bees released a beeswax-based balm in 1991, and EOS introduced a spherical balm in 2011 [2].

Lip scrubs developed as part of the wider market for exfoliating products, which Wikipedia's exfoliation article divides into mechanical methods (cloths, scrubs, crushed shells, sugar or salt crystals, pumice, sponges, brushes) and chemical methods using hydroxy acids or enzymes [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and appearance routines
paras: Lips matter to appearance because the red vermilion zone and the Cupid's bow define the lower face, and Wikipedia's lip article notes survey-based links between lip fullness and attractiveness while flagging the sourcing as weak.[3] Lip scrubs fit into the broader lip-care routine of scrub, balm and colour.[2][3]
A T Nation poster describes lips that 'never heal' and develop a layer of dead skin that has to be removed, an example of the dry-lip complaint that scrubbing is meant to address.[5]

Over-exfoliation of skin is described as capable of impairing the barrier and increasing tightness, sensitivity, dryness and infection risk.[1] In exfoliative cheilitis, a rare condition with scaling lips, a link to lip picking or licking habits has been reported.[4]

Wikipedia's lip balm article reports debate among physicians about whether some balms dry the lips or encourage repeated reapplication, with one dermatologist quoted as saying some ingredients can irritate sensitive lips and another linking flavour-licking to dependence; a Snopes review is reported to have found no evidence for extreme claims about Carmex [2]. It also notes that a 2015 German consumer test reported mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons in mineral-oil-based lip products, which European food authorities consider possibly carcinogenic, and that a 2015 study showing a lip balm improved barrier function was funded by Burt's Bees [2]. Allergic contact cheilitis is most often triggered by lip cosmetics, then toothpaste, and patch testing can identify the cause [4].

Actinic cheilitis, caused by long-term sun exposure and usually affecting the lower lip, appears as dry, scaly, wrinkled skin and carries a small long-term risk of squamous cell carcinoma [4]. Lip skin that stays scaly or sore is therefore described in medical sources as something clinicians can assess [4].

Lip scrubs are a staple of beauty-routine content, are sold by cosmetics and skin-care brands, and are commonly made at home from kitchen ingredients. Forum discussion in the looksmaxxing and lifting sphere is sparse; the most relevant T Nation post is a user describing lips that never heal and form a layer of dead skin [5]. Lip fullness and the Cupid's bow are widely discussed in appearance communities, and Wikipedia's lip article notes survey-based links between lip fullness and attractiveness while flagging the sourcing [3].

lore.intro: Lip exfoliation appears in beauty routines more than in looksmaxxing forums, where dry lips are mentioned in passing [5].
